The People Who Vouch for You

Playbooklowob research

By lowob · 24 June 2026 · 7-minute read · Growth

In fintech, your community is the practitioners who advise your segment and the customers willing to be named. Give them a job, pay them openly where the rules allow, and measure referred funded accounts. The evidence that referrals are worth building is good: a study of about 10,000 customers at a German bank found referred customers were at least 16% more valuable over six years and less likely to leave. The rules are specific too. The FTC bans rewards conditioned on positive reviews, the FCA treats some practitioner posts as financial promotions, and in some products, such as US mortgage settlement services, paying for referrals is prohibited outright.

This is strategic guidance from go-to-market work, not legal or regulatory advice.

Who the community actually is

Trust is the product set out the order buyers check: who is behind it, who holds the money, who else like me uses it. The third question is answered by people, not copy.

In fintech those people fall into two groups. Practitioners: accountants, bookkeepers, advisers, fractional finance leads, payroll bureaus. And users: the treasury team, the small-business owner, the operations manager who lives in your product.

Neither group wants a server to hang out in. They want to look competent in front of their clients and their boards. Your product either helps with that or it does not. So drop the word community if it leads you to build a chat room. Build a vouching system instead.

The job, applied to fintech

Community is a job, not a number said give the community a job before you count it. In fintech there are three jobs, and each is measurable.

Referrals. A practitioner who recommends you to a client is the cheapest route to a funded account you will find. Distribute through whoever already holds the customer covered the channel economics. The academic evidence supports the bet. Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte tracked about 10,000 customers of a German bank for almost three years. Referred customers had a higher contribution margin at first, a retention advantage that persisted, and an average value at least 16% higher than other customers. The bank paid a €25 voucher per referral, and the authors estimated a return of about 60% on it over six years.

Product feedback from power users. A treasury team that reconciles daily will find your edge cases before your QA does. A small-business owner will tell you what the onboarding form got wrong. Both are worth more than a survey.

Public trust signals. Reviews on the platforms your segment reads. References you can hand to a procurement team. Complaints answered in public, quickly.

JobOwnerCadenceNumber
ReferralsPartnerships leadMonthly review per practitionerReferred funded accounts and their 90- and 365-day retention
Product feedbackProduct leadQuarterly advisory group, plus a standing channelIssues raised that shipped
Trust signalsCustomer or marketing leadWeekly review responseResponse time; named references available

Each job gets an owner, a cadence and a number. That is the whole difference between a community and a mailing list.

The first hundred, fintech version

The first hundred described the first hundred members as people chosen on purpose. For fintech the composition is specific.

Eighty practitioners who advise your target segment. Not followers. People who sit with your customers and are asked "what should I use for this?"

Twenty customers willing to be named. Named means a logo, a quote, a reference call, or a case study with a real number in it. Each of the twenty should map to one of the beliefs in the claims register described in Trust is the product.

Recruit the practitioners first. A practitioner who already trusts you brings the named customers with them.

The practitioner programme

A practitioner programme has four parts. Keep it that simple.

Education. Short, useful sessions on the problem, not the product. How to run client treasury. What changes when a client crosses a payment threshold. Practitioners share things that make them look sharp.

Early access. Let them see a feature before their clients ask about it. It costs you nothing and makes them the person who knew first.

A direct line. One named person they can message when a client is stuck. Not a ticket queue. This single thing does more than any incentive.

Payment. Pay per funded account if you choose to, and disclose it to the client every time. A referral fee that is hidden becomes a trust problem the day it surfaces. One that is disclosed is how the market works. The research suggests rewards earn their keep in exactly this setting: in Ryu and Feick's experiments, offering a reward raised referral likelihood by more than 20 percentage points for a weaker brand, and mattered most between people with weak ties.

A referral fee that is hidden becomes a trust problem the day it surfaces. One that is disclosed is how the market works.

Disclosure is the minimum, and some rules go further. Check the referrer's own rules and the product's before agreeing terms. Our Referral partners without leakage covers registering, paying and disclosing introductions so the economics and the trust both hold.

Who refersRule to checkWhat it asks
UK chartered accountantsICAEW Code of Ethics and guidanceObtain client consent and notify clients of the amounts received

Anyone referring US mortgage settlement businessRESPA Section 8 (Regulation X, 12 CFR 1024.14)Fees for referrals are prohibited

For small-business and institutional products, add a user advisory group: six to ten customers, quarterly, with a roadmap in front of them. They tell you what to build. You tell them what you decided and why.

Reviews and complaints as infrastructure

Review platforms are part of the vouching system whether you manage them or not. Someone will check. Claim the profile, respond to every review, and ask satisfied customers to post without offering anything for it.

Complaint handling is the other half. A complaint answered in public, within hours, with a clear fix, is a trust asset. A buyer reading it learns how you behave when something goes wrong, which is the fourth question in the buyer's order, answered by evidence. Build the process before you need it: who sees the complaint, who answers, how fast, and what they are allowed to say.

The lines you don't cross

Some things turn a community asset into a liability overnight.

No incentivised reviews. The FTC's rule on consumer reviews and testimonials, in force since 21 October 2024, prohibits paying or rewarding reviews that express a particular sentiment. A small reward for any honest review is not inherently unlawful, but a discount for a five-star review is. The FTC's guidance puts it plainly: "You can't condition an incentive, for example a discount, on a review being positive." Penalties can reach $51,744 per violation, adjusted annually.

No testimonial you cannot substantiate. If a named customer says they saved a number, you need the number in a file.

Nothing that reads as a financial promotion without approval. A practitioner's post about your yield product may be a promotion in your regulator's eyes. The FCA's FG24/1 says firms working with affiliates should take proactive responsibility and remain responsible for every promotion they make or cause to be made. Give practitioners approved wording and a review step.

Then measure the thing that matters: referred funded accounts, by practitioner and by channel, and their 90-day and 365-day retention. Referrals that fund and stay are the only proof the community is doing its job.

lowob takeaways

  • Recruit eighty practitioners and twenty named customers. Practitioners first; they bring the customers.
  • Give each job an owner, a cadence and a number. Referrals, feedback and trust signals.
  • Pay openly, and check the rules first. Disclosure is the minimum; some referrers need client consent and some products ban referral fees.
  • Never reward sentiment. Ask for honest reviews and offer nothing tied to the rating.
  • Measure referred funded accounts and their retention. By practitioner, at 90 and 365 days.

Common questions

How should a fintech company build a community?

Build a vouching system of practitioners, such as accountants, bookkeepers and advisers, and named customers. Give it three measurable jobs: referrals, product feedback and public trust signals.

Can fintechs pay accountants or advisers for referrals?

Often, but check the rules first and disclose the payment every time. UK chartered accountants must obtain client consent and notify amounts received; promoters of US investment advisers must disclose compensation; referral fees for US mortgage settlement services are prohibited.

Can I offer customers a discount for a five-star review?

No. In the US, the FTC's 2024 rule prohibits rewarding reviews that express a particular sentiment. Ask satisfied customers to post honestly without tying anything to the rating.

Are referred customers more valuable for a bank or fintech?

The best evidence says yes. A study of about 10,000 customers at a German bank found referred customers had higher early margins, lower churn and at least 16% higher value over six years.

Sources and notes

  • Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte, Referral Programs and Customer Value, Journal of Marketing, 2011. Academic study of one German bank, 2006 to 2008.
  • Baylor University Keller Center, Referral reward programs and referral likelihood, 2008. Summary of Ryu and Feick's Journal of Marketing experiments; secondary summary of the paper.
  • FTC, Trade Regulation Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials, Federal Register, 22 August 2024. Final rule, effective 21 October 2024; US only.
  • Morgan Lewis, FTC Issues Final Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials, August 2024. Law firm summary; source for the sentiment test and penalty figure.
  • FTC, Endorsement Guides: What People Are Asking, last updated July 2025. Staff guidance, not a rule.
  • ICAEW, Commissions and fees: fully informed consent, 8 January 2025. Professional body guidance for its members.
  • SEC, Investment Adviser Marketing: small entity compliance guide, accessed November 2026. Applies to SEC-registered investment advisers.
  • CFPB, Regulation X, 12 CFR 1024.14: Prohibition against kickbacks and unearned fees, accessed November 2026. Regulation text; mortgage settlement services only.
  • FCA, FG24/1 Finalised guidance on financial promotions on social media, 26 March 2024. UK regulator guidance.
